title: Jury reaches decision in Mahoney inquest
article: The jury tasked with examining the circumstances that led to Matthew Mahoney's fatal interaction with two Windsor police officers has determined the 33-year-old's death was a homicide.

In a decision Friday afternoon, the five-person jury declared Mahoney's March 21, 2018 shooting death was due to police action - a lawful killing by police - rather than a suicide by police or an undeterminable manner of death.
This decision does not change the results of an investigation by Ontario's Special Investigations Unit that cleared Windsor police of wrongdoing.
"I want to thank and commend you the jury for your thoughtful questions and high quality of your recommendations," said Daniel Ambrosini, the inquest's presiding officer.
"To the Mahoney family, we thank you for your participation, as difficult as it was. We acknowledge again the loss of your son, brother, and friend."

The jury's verdict also included nine recommendations for the Ministry of Health, the provincial government, the Ministry of the Solicitor General, the Windsor Police Service, and Windsor Regional Hospital to prevent similar deaths in the future.

The Ministry of Health, the jury determined, should collect and publish non-identifying data about wait times for treatment and patient volumes, as well as days and hours of mental health services provided, all to assist clinicians in "directing patients to receive timely mental health services," and "promoting accountability of community mental health services."

The ministry should also give hospitals and community-based mental health services the resources to provide such data, and the resources to increase mental health awareness and promotion of initiatives to address the "lack of familiarity" with services and options available "for persons and families dealing with mental health situations."
Mahoney died downtown more than four years ago after being shot by police multiple times.

The fatal shooting that day in March began with a 911 call about a man carrying a knife block with multiple knives in Windsor's core. Mahoney, who had a history of mental illness and had been diagnosed with schizophrenia, reportedly slashed at one officer.
Officers attempted to use a Taser, which was ineffective. Officers were retreating when Mahoney continued to advance, brandishing a knife. That's when officers reportedly fired shots.

The jury recommended that the Ministry of Health strike a task force within six months of the jury's verdict to review, report on, and initiate changes to several aspects of the mental-health services it funds. Those aspects include funding, accountabilities, and timely access to care for all community-based mental health services; available resources and supports for family members and/or caregivers of patients receiving mental health services; how family members and caregivers and community services can provide support and information and patients when patient consent is not provided; address what information can be shared from family members and other stakeholders; and align services and community agencies to better share information about individuals with mental health concerns in the community.

The task force, the jury said, should focus these reviews on the "most vulnerable patients," particularly those diagnosed with moderate to severe mental illness, "especially schizophrenia and/or schizophrenia-related disorders."

The jury's third and final recommendation for the Ministry of Health was to establish further study and review of criteria and training associated with the Mental Health Act. It should report on recommendations to address mandatory refresher training for emergency room physicians and psychiatrists, and to address the assessment of specific criteria for psychiatric evaluation and involuntary detention. It should also determine how best to ensure collateral information from family members and relevant community services can be included as part of the process for determining treatment options.

The provincial government, the jury said, should "offer and arrange enhanced legal and mental health support" for families of people who die in a police encounter, and "ensure that those services are delivered in a timely and trauma-informed manner."

For Windsor police and the Ministry of the Solicitor General, it's recommended that both provide enhanced police training to address mental health-related situations and crises, including awareness education to recognize and identify situations where mental illness may play a role.

The Windsor Police Service should review resources allocated to its Community Outreach and Support Team (COAST) program to offer increased 24/7 support based on the growing community mental health needs in Windsor.

The jury recommended that Windsor Regional Hospital continue ongoing quality assessments "to drive continuous improvements," particularly to best practices for mental health services. Reviews and audits of core services should occur annually, the jury said.
The hospital should also assess the feasibility and impact of establishing a mental health advocate to be the "point person" helping patients and families co-ordinate mental health services.
